title: Los Angeles with his brother, being a has-been, and today's New Orleans bands
summary: He describes the Hollywood musicians' clique and Frank Segrest, then comments on the Dixieland band on Bourbon Street, Raymond Burke, Alvin Alcorn and the trombonist.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Burton was his grandfather's name. But she called him at the time, he did seem to like Jews. So he had his name changed to Victor Burton. And incidentally, he got with Alfred Newman, the second drummer, and my brother. And when he found out that my brother was Paul G. D. D. D. D. D. D. D., they were buddy-buddy. I mean his job was secure. You know how he clicked together. The first week I went out to Los Angeles, I must have had dinner in a hundred musicians' houses. They all take me to get acquainted. It's a clique. And it's good to be in the clique. And even if they don't know you, they say they do. I remember Frank Segrest, one of the finest drummers. Have you ever heard of him? Yeah. He didn't know me. He didn't know me. But I knew Segrest's reputation. He knew of my reputation. And when I went out to the Chinese theater with my brother, my brother was playing the Footlight Parade, Jimmy Cagney, just a presentation. Just a, did very little orchestra, played the music, and they did something on the stage. But I'm stuck in a Waterville theater, and I said, if I'm going back to Waterville, I'm going back to New Orleans. But I go up there, and there's San Frank Segrest, he sees Paul, and there comes Johnny. He picks me up, and Johnny, my boy, and he swings me along, and I'm his loving pal, going on a man for a matter. I said, Paul, who is the guy? He's a Segrest. Oh, I said, well, I'm out of him. But that's the way it is. Today, even in this building, they say, you know Johnny Detroit. They don't say, this is Mr. Detroit, because the people might not know me. And I don't know them. And how I find out their name, I ask them their apartment number. Then I go look on the ball. Because they said that they dance to my music when they're young. And they're mostly widows, too, to talk. So, you know Sam, you know Joe, Joe, who, what, Joe, I don't know. So I go look. But it's one of those things. To be a, what would you say, a semi-celebrity, a has-been. The only thing I gratified myself is that I, it's better to be a has-been than I never was. And I'm still, I meet lots of people. And now here's the strange thing, I never blew a note on Bourbon Street in my life. Never blew a note on Bourbon Street. Congratulations. You betcha, I congratulate myself too, aren't ya? But there's a fine band in that, your father's mustache. I want to tell you that. Have you heard him lately? Who is that?
I know that this old-timer that played the clanner with everybody and his brother, he can't read much. Raymond Burke.

Well, you might say he's the weakest man in the band. But they have a colored trumpet player, he gets my vote. Alvin Alcorn. What's his name? Alvin Alcorn. You could tell him I like his trumpet player.
I will, next time I go there.

And you tell the trombone player he's got plenty of power, which is a little too much. He knocked me out of the window. But he plays, brother, he plays. And when you play with that assertion, you can, don't you like these trombone players? Oh, yeah.
